category: Numerical Methods II: Solver Options, Events & Extended Optimization
description: The common numerical-control options (AccuracyGoal, PrecisionGoal, MaxSteps, Method, monitors), event handling and parametric solving for NDSolve, stochastic differential equations, polynomial root isolation, value/argument variants of the optimizers, combinatorial optimization (knapsack, shortest tour), and numerical limits, derivatives and residues.

tools.name: AccuracyGoal
tools.description: Option of NIntegrate, NDSolve, FindRoot, FindMinimum, NSum, NMinimize and other numerical functions specifying the number of digits of absolute accuracy sought (error <= 10^-AccuracyGoal); PrecisionGoal specifies relative precision. The result is accepted when either goal is met, so set AccuracyGoal -> Infinity to require relative precision only (important when the true answer may be zero or very small).
tools.usage:
NIntegrate[f, {x, a, b}, AccuracyGoal -> 10, PrecisionGoal -> 10]
NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, T}, AccuracyGoal -> 12, PrecisionGoal -> 12, WorkingPrecision -> 20]
FindRoot[eq, {x, x0}, AccuracyGoal -> 8]

parameters.name: AccuracyGoal
parameters.description: Digits of absolute accuracy (Automatic ~ half of WorkingPrecision).

tools.example: NIntegrate[Exp[-x^2], {x, -Infinity, Infinity}, PrecisionGoal -> 12, WorkingPrecision -> 30]
tools.notes: Goals cannot exceed WorkingPrecision; raise WorkingPrecision above MachinePrecision (e.g. 30) for high-accuracy results.

tools.name: MaxSteps
tools.description: NDSolve option bounding the number of integration steps (default 10000 per dimension, Automatic); NDSolve::mxst warns when exceeded, typically because of stiffness or a singularity. Related step controls: MaxStepSize, StartingStepSize, MaxStepFraction (max fraction of the interval per step), and InterpolationOrder for the returned InterpolatingFunction.
tools.usage:
NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, T}, MaxSteps -> 10^6]
NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, T}, MaxStepSize -> 0.01]
NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, T}, MaxSteps -> Infinity, InterpolationOrder -> All]

parameters.name: MaxStepSize
parameters.description: Largest step; use to resolve fast forcing terms.

parameters.name: InterpolationOrder
parameters.description: All keeps the integrator's full-order dense output.

tools.name: Method
tools.description: The universal option selecting an algorithm. NDSolve: "ExplicitRungeKutta", "ImplicitRungeKutta", "BDF", "Adams", "StiffnessSwitching", "IDA" (DAEs), "SymplecticPartitionedRungeKutta", "Extrapolation", "EventLocator", "Projection", {"MethodOfLines", ...}, {"FiniteElement", ...}. NIntegrate: "GlobalAdaptive", "LocalAdaptive", "DoubleExponential", "MonteCarlo", "QuasiMonteCarlo", rules such as "GaussKronrodRule", "ClenshawCurtisRule", "LevinRule", "TrapezoidalRule". FindMinimum: "Newton", "QuasiNewton", "ConjugateGradient", "PrincipalAxis", "LevenbergMarquardt", "InteriorPoint". NMinimize: "NelderMead", "DifferentialEvolution", "SimulatedAnnealing", "RandomSearch". Sub-options are given as {"name", opt -> val}.
tools.usage:
NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, T}, Method -> "StiffnessSwitching"]
NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, T}, Method -> {"ExplicitRungeKutta", "DifferenceOrder" -> 8}]
NIntegrate[f, {x, 0, 1}, Method -> {"GlobalAdaptive", Method -> "GaussKronrodRule"}]
FindMinimum[f, {x, x0}, Method -> "Newton"]
NMinimize[f, vars, Method -> {"DifferentialEvolution", "SearchPoints" -> 100}]

parameters.name: Method
parameters.description: Method name string, or {"name", suboptions...}; Automatic chooses by problem structure.

tools.example:
NIntegrate[Sin[1000 x] Exp[-x], {x, 0, 10}, Method -> "LevinRule"] (* oscillatory *)
NDSolve[{y'[t] == -1000 (y[t] - Cos[t]), y[0] == 0}, y, {t, 0, 10}, Method -> "BDF"] (* stiff *)

tools.name: StepMonitor
tools.description: StepMonitor :> expr evaluates expr after every accepted step of NDSolve, FindRoot, FindMinimum, NMinimize, NIntegrate etc. (with the current variable values in scope), and EvaluationMonitor :> expr after every function evaluation. Combine with Sow/Reap to record convergence paths or with Monitor for progress display.
tools.usage:
FindRoot[f[x] == 0, {x, x0}, StepMonitor :> Sow[x]]
Reap[NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, T}, StepMonitor :> Sow[t]]]
NIntegrate[f[x], {x, 0, 1}, EvaluationMonitor :> Sow[x]]

parameters.name: StepMonitor
parameters.description: Held expression run once per step.

parameters.name: EvaluationMonitor
parameters.description: Held expression run at every evaluation of the objective.

tools.example:
{sol, path} = Reap[FindMinimum[(x - 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2 + x y, {{x, 0}, {y, 0}}, StepMonitor :> Sow[{x, y}]]];
ListLinePlot[path[[1]], PlotMarkers -> Automatic]
tools.notes: Use :> (RuleDelayed), never ->, so the expression is evaluated at each step rather than once.

tools.name: WhenEvent
tools.description: WhenEvent[event, action] inside NDSolve specifies discrete events: when event (a condition becoming true, a zero crossing of an expression, Mod[t, dt] == 0 for periodic events) occurs, action is executed - reset state variables (y[t] -> -0.9 y[t]), change a DiscreteVariables value, record with Sow, or stop with "StopIntegration". It is the mechanism for bouncing balls, switching systems, impulses and hybrid models.
tools.usage:
NDSolve[{eqs, WhenEvent[cond, action]}, vars, {t, 0, T}]
WhenEvent[y[t] == 0, y'[t] -> -0.8 y'[t]]
WhenEvent[t == 5, {x[t] -> x[t] + 1}]
WhenEvent[Mod[t, 1] == 0, Sow[{t, y[t]}]]
WhenEvent[x[t] > 10, "StopIntegration"]

parameters.name: event
parameters.description: Condition or equation whose crossing triggers the event; "DetectionMethod" and "LocationMethod" sub-options refine detection.

parameters.name: action
parameters.description: Rules assigning new values, a string action ("StopIntegration", "RemoveEvent", "RestartIntegration"), or any expression.

tools.example:
ball = NDSolveValue[{y''[t] == -9.81, y[0] == 10, y'[0] == 0, WhenEvent[y[t] == 0, y'[t] -> -0.9 y'[t]]}, y, {t, 0, 10}];
Plot[ball[t], {t, 0, 10}]
(* discrete counter *)
NDSolve[{x'[t] == -x[t], x[0] == 1, n[0] == 0, WhenEvent[Mod[t, 1] == 0, n[t] -> n[t] + 1]}, {x, n}, {t, 0, 5}, DiscreteVariables -> {n}]

tools.name: DiscreteVariables
tools.description: NDSolve option declaring variables that change only at WhenEvent actions (piecewise-constant state such as counters, modes or gear settings); DependentVariables lists the unknown functions explicitly when they cannot be inferred. Together with WhenEvent they let NDSolve handle hybrid discrete/continuous systems.
tools.usage:
NDSolve[{eqs, WhenEvent[...]}, {x, mode}, {t, 0, T}, DiscreteVariables -> {mode \[Element] {0, 1}}]
NDSolve[eqs, vars, range, DependentVariables -> {x, y}]

parameters.name: DiscreteVariables
parameters.description: List of variables (optionally with domains) updated only by events.

tools.example:
thermostat = NDSolveValue[{T'[t] == If[h[t] == 1, 2, -1] (1 + 0 T[t]), T[0] == 20, h[0] == 1,
   WhenEvent[T[t] > 22, h[t] -> 0], WhenEvent[T[t] < 18, h[t] -> 1]}, T, {t, 0, 30}, DiscreteVariables -> {h}]

tools.name: ParametricNDSolve
tools.description: Solves a differential system depending on symbolic parameters, returning a ParametricFunction that yields the InterpolatingFunction for any parameter values (with derivatives w.r.t. parameters available) - ideal for parameter sweeps, fitting ODE models to data (NonlinearModelFit on the parametric solution) and sensitivity analysis. ParametricNDSolveValue is listed in the calculus chunk; this is the rule-returning form.
tools.usage:
ParametricNDSolve[eqs, {y1, y2, ...}, {t, tmin, tmax}, {p1, p2, ...}]
sol[pvals]

parameters.name: eqs
parameters.description: Equations and initial conditions containing the parameters.

tools.name: ItoProcess
tools.description: Represents a stochastic differential equation in Ito form dx = a dt + b dW (StratonovichProcess for the Stratonovich interpretation) with drift, diffusion and initial value; RandomFunction simulates paths (Euler-Maruyama and higher-order methods via Method), and Mean/Variance/CovarianceFunction/PDF give exact or approximate moments. Use them for finance (GBM, OU), physics (Langevin) and noisy control models.
tools.usage:
ItoProcess[{a, b}, {x, x0}, t]
ItoProcess[{dx == a dt + b dw, x[t0] == x0}, x[t], t]
StratonovichProcess[{a, b}, {x, x0}, t]
RandomFunction[proc, {t0, t1, dt}, n]
tools.notes: GeometricBrownianMotionProcess and OrnsteinUhlenbeckProcess are predefined special cases.

tools.name: InterpolatingFunction
tools.description: The object returned by NDSolve, Interpolation, ListInterpolation and FunctionInterpolation representing a numerically tabulated function with interpolation; it can be evaluated, differentiated (f'), integrated (Integrate/NIntegrate), plotted and queried for its "Domain", "Grid", "ValuesOnGrid" and "InterpolationOrder". Understanding it is key to post-processing NDSolve output.
tools.usage:
f = NDSolveValue[...]
f[t]
f'[t]
f["Domain"]
f["Grid"]
f["ValuesOnGrid"]
FunctionInterpolation[expr, {x, xmin, xmax}]
tools.example:
y = NDSolveValue[{y'[t] == Cos[t] y[t], y[0] == 1}, y, {t, 0, 10}];
y["Domain"] (* {{0., 10.}} *)
NIntegrate[y[t], {t, 0, 10}]
Export["sol.csv", Transpose[{First[y["Grid"]] // Flatten, y["ValuesOnGrid"]}]]
tools.notes: Evaluating outside the domain extrapolates with a warning (InterpolatingFunction::dmval); use "ExtrapolationHandler" to change that.

tools.name: NRoots
tools.description: Numerically finds all roots of a univariate polynomial equation (methods "Aberth", "CompanionMatrix", "JenkinsTraub"), returning a disjunction of equations; CountRoots counts real (or complex-region) roots exactly, RootIntervals isolates real roots in disjoint intervals and IsolatingInterval isolates a given Root object. Use them for reliable polynomial root finding when NSolve's generality is unnecessary.
tools.usage:
NRoots[poly == 0, x]
NRoots[poly == 0, x, n]
CountRoots[poly, x]
CountRoots[poly, {x, a, b}]
RootIntervals[poly]
IsolatingInterval[Root[...]]
tools.example:
NRoots[x^5 - 3 x + 1 == 0, x]
CountRoots[x^5 - 3 x + 1, {x, 0, 1}] (* 1 *)
RootIntervals[x^5 - 3 x + 1]

tools.name: FindMinValue
tools.description: Value-only and argument-only variants of the local optimizers: FindMinValue/FindMaxValue return just the optimal value and FindArgMax the maximizing point (FindArgMin is already listed), avoiding the {value, rules} pair of FindMinimum. Same options and Method choices as FindMinimum, including constraints.
tools.usage:
FindMinValue[f, {x, x0}]
FindMinValue[{f, cons}, {{x, x0}, {y, y0}}]
FindMaxValue[f, {x, x0}]
FindArgMax[f, {x, x0}]

tools.name: NMinValue
tools.description: Global numerical optimization returning only the value (NMinValue, NMaxValue) or only the argument (NArgMin, NArgMax), the NMinimize-family analogues of FindMinValue/FindArgMin; MinValue/MaxValue are the exact symbolic counterparts of Minimize/Maximize. Useful in nested optimization where the rules form is inconvenient.
tools.usage:
NMinValue[f, {x, y}]
NMinValue[{f, cons}, {x, y}]
NArgMin[f, {x, y}]
NArgMax[{f, cons}, vars]
MinValue[{f, cons}, vars]
MaxValue[f, x]
tools.example:
NArgMin[{x^2 + y^2, x + y >= 1}, {x, y}] (* {0.5, 0.5} *)
MinValue[{x^2 + y^2, x + y == 1}, {x, y}] (* 1/2 *)
NMaxValue[Sin[x] + Cos[2 x], x]

tools.name: GeometricOptimization
tools.description: Solves geometric programs (posynomial objective and constraints, variables positive) by transforming to convex form - used in circuit sizing, structural design and chemical engineering. Part of the convex optimization family with LinearFractionalOptimization (ratio of affine functions subject to linear constraints), both returning optimal values or argument rules like the other *Optimization functions.
tools.usage:
GeometricOptimization[f, cons, vars]
GeometricOptimization[f, cons, vars, "prop"]
LinearFractionalOptimization[{alpha, beta}/{gamma, delta}, {a, b}, x]
LinearFractionalOptimization[f, cons, vars]

parameters.name: cons
parameters.description: Posynomial <= 1 or monomial == 1 constraints, or linear constraints.

tools.example:
GeometricOptimization[x/y + y/z + z/x, {x y z == 1, x >= 1/2}, {x, y, z}]
LinearFractionalOptimization[(x + 2 y + 1)/(x + y + 2), {x >= 0, y >= 0, x + y <= 5}, {x, y}]

tools.name: DualLinearProgramming
tools.description: Solves a linear program and its dual simultaneously, returning {x, y, u, v} (primal solution, dual variables, and bound multipliers) in the same matrix form as LinearProgramming. Useful for sensitivity analysis and shadow prices; the modern LinearOptimization gives the same via "DualMaximizer" and "ConstraintSensitivity" properties.
tools.usage:
DualLinearProgramming[c, m, b]
DualLinearProgramming[c, m, b, l]
LinearOptimization[f, cons, vars, {"PrimalMinimizer", "DualMaximizer"}]

parameters.name: m, b
parameters.description: Constraint matrix and right-hand side (m.x >= b).

tools.example:
DualLinearProgramming[{1, 1}, {{1, 2}, {3, 1}}, {4, 6}]
LinearOptimization[x + y, {x + 2 y >= 4, 3 x + y >= 6}, {x, y}, {"PrimalMinimizer", "DualMaximizer", "ConstraintSensitivity"}]

tools.name: KnapsackSolve
tools.description: Solves 0-1, bounded and unbounded knapsack problems: choose item counts maximizing total value subject to capacity constraints on one or more cost dimensions. Items are given as {cost, value, maxcount} triples or an association; the result is a list/association of counts. A convenient front end to integer LinearOptimization for allocation problems.
tools.usage:
KnapsackSolve[{{cost1, val1, max1}, ...}, capacity]
KnapsackSolve[<|"item" -> {cost, val, max}, ...|>, capacity]
KnapsackSolve[{{{c11, c12}, val1, max1}, ...}, {cap1, cap2}]

parameters.name: items
parameters.description: Cost, value and maximum count per item (max may be Infinity).

parameters.name: capacity
parameters.description: Total cost allowed (vector for multiple resources).

tools.example:
KnapsackSolve[<|"tent" -> {5, 10, 1}, "stove" -> {3, 7, 1}, "food" -> {1, 2, Infinity}|>, 10]
(* <|"tent" -> 1, "stove" -> 1, "food" -> 2|> *)

tools.name: FindShortestTour
tools.description: Finds a short closed tour through a set of points (travelling salesman) or graph vertices, returning {length, ordering}; methods include exact solving for small n and heuristics ("Greedy", "TwoOpt", "OrTools", "SimulatedAnnealing") for large n, with DistanceFunction for custom metrics and geo positions. Use it for routing, PCB drill paths and plotter optimisation.
tools.usage:
FindShortestTour[{p1, p2, ...}]
FindShortestTour[{p1, ...}, start, end]
FindShortestTour[graph]
FindShortestTour[pts, Method -> "TwoOpt", DistanceFunction -> ManhattanDistance]

parameters.name: start, end
parameters.description: Optional fixed endpoints for an open path.

tools.name: FindPeaks
tools.description: Finds local maxima {position, value} in a list (or TimeSeries), with optional Gaussian smoothing scale sigma, minimum sharpness s and threshold t to suppress noise. The standard tool for peak detection in spectra, chromatograms and signals; apply to -list to find valleys.
tools.usage:
FindPeaks[list]
FindPeaks[list, sigma]
FindPeaks[list, sigma, s]
FindPeaks[list, sigma, s, t]

tools.name: FindFormula
tools.description: Symbolic regression: searches for a closed-form function f[x] that fits {x, y} data, returning the best candidate or the n best with fit quality, optionally restricted to given target functions. Use it for empirical law discovery when the model form is unknown; verify with NonlinearModelFit.
tools.usage:
FindFormula[data, x]
FindFormula[data, x, n]
FindFormula[data, x, n, prop]
FindFormula[data, x, TargetFunctions -> {Exp, Log, Power}]

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: List of {x, y} pairs (or y values with implicit x = 1, 2, ...).

tools.notes: Introduced in 10.2; results are heuristic and not guaranteed unique.

tools.name: NLimit
tools.description: Numerical limit of an expression as x -> x0 using sequence extrapolation, for cases where Limit cannot produce a closed form; ND gives numerical derivatives of any order with Richardson extrapolation, NSeries a numerical Laurent/Taylor series and NResidue a numerical residue. All four live in the NumericalCalculus` package, which must be loaded with Needs first (they are not system symbols).
tools.usage:
Needs["NumericalCalculus`"]
NLimit[expr, x -> x0]
ND[expr, x, x0]
ND[expr, {x, n}, x0]
NSeries[f, {z, z0, n}]
NResidue[f, {z, z0}]
tools.example:
Needs["NumericalCalculus`"];
NLimit[Sin[x]/x, x -> 0]
ND[BesselJ[0, x], x, 1.5]
ND[Exp[x^2], {x, 3}, 0.5, Terms -> 10]
tools.notes: Package functions: documentation is under the NumericalCalculus package section, not the main reference. For symbolic derivatives use D; for black-box functions ND uses finite differences with extrapolation (Method -> "EulerSum" or "NIntegrate").

tools.name: NFourierTransform
tools.description: Numerically evaluates the continuous Fourier transform of a function at a given frequency (with NInverseFourierTransform, NFourierSinTransform, NFourierCosTransform and NFourierCoefficient / NFourierSeries for numerical Fourier series) using adaptive quadrature, with the same FourierParameters conventions as FourierTransform. These are functions of the FourierSeries` package (load with Needs); use them when the symbolic transform is unavailable or the function is only known numerically.
tools.usage:
Needs["FourierSeries`"]
NFourierTransform[expr, t, omega]
NInverseFourierTransform[expr, omega, t]
NFourierTransform[expr, t, omega, FourierParameters -> {0, -2 Pi}]
NFourierCoefficient[expr, t, n]

parameters.name: omega
parameters.description: Numeric frequency at which to evaluate.

tools.notes: Package functions (FourierSeries`), not system symbols. For sampled data use Fourier (DFT) instead.

tools.name: GreenFunction
tools.description: Computes the Green's function of a linear ODE or PDE operator with boundary conditions over a region, allowing the solution for any source term by integration. Use it for symbolic boundary-value analysis, impulse responses and constructing solutions of Poisson/heat/wave problems.
tools.usage:
GreenFunction[{op[y[x]], bcs}, y[x], {x, a, b}, xs]
GreenFunction[{op[u[x, t]], bcs}, u[x, t], {x, t} \[Element] reg, {xs, ts}]

parameters.name: op[y[x]]
parameters.description: Linear differential operator applied to y.

tools.example:
g = GreenFunction[{-y''[x], y[0] == 0, y[1] == 0}, y[x], {x, 0, 1}, s]
sol[x_] = Integrate[g f[s], {s, 0, 1}] (* solves -y'' = f with y(0)=y(1)=0 *)

tools.name: DifferentialRoot
tools.description: Represents a function implicitly as the solution of a linear ODE with initial conditions (holonomic representation), as returned by DSolve for equations without closed forms; DifferentialRootReduce converts special functions and expressions to this form, and DifferenceRoot/DifferenceRootReduce are the recurrence analogues. Evaluate, differentiate, expand in series and plot them like any function.
tools.usage:
DifferentialRoot[Function[{y, x}, {ode, y[x0] == y0, y'[x0] == y1}]][x]
DifferentialRootReduce[expr, x]
DifferenceRoot[Function[{y, n}, {rec, y[0] == a0, y[1] == a1}]][n]
DifferenceRootReduce[expr, n]

parameters.name: ode / rec
parameters.description: Linear differential or difference equation with polynomial coefficients.

tools.example:
DifferentialRootReduce[AiryAi[x] + Exp[x], x]
f = DifferentialRoot[Function[{y, x}, {y''[x] + x y[x] == 0, y[0] == 1, y'[0] == 0}]];
Plot[f[x], {x, 0, 10}]
Series[f[x], {x, 0, 6}]

tools.name: InverseFunction
tools.description: Represents the inverse of a function; known inverses evaluate immediately (InverseFunction[Sin] gives ArcSin) and unknown ones remain symbolic but can be applied and evaluated numerically via FindRoot-style inversion inside N, Plot and Solve. Solve returns InverseFunction objects for transcendental equations without named inverses.
tools.usage:
InverseFunction[f]
InverseFunction[f][y]
InverseFunction[f, n, m]

parameters.name: n, m
parameters.description: Invert with respect to argument n of an m-argument function.

tools.example:
InverseFunction[Tanh] (* ArcTanh *)
g = InverseFunction[#^3 + # &];
g[10] // N (* 2.00... root of x^3 + x = 10 *)
Solve[x Exp[x] == 2, x] (* uses ProductLog *)

tools.name: BayesianMinimization
tools.description: Global optimization of an expensive black-box function (e.g. a simulation or model-training run) using Bayesian optimization with a Gaussian-process surrogate; BayesianMaximization is the mirror. Returns a BayesianMinimizationObject with "MinimumConfiguration", "MinimumValue" and the sampled history. Use it for hyperparameter tuning and design of experiments with few evaluations.
tools.usage:
BayesianMinimization[f, {conf1, conf2, ...}]
BayesianMinimization[f, reg]
BayesianMinimization[f, sampler, MaxIterations -> n]
obj["MinimumConfiguration"]

parameters.name: f
parameters.description: Function of a configuration returning a real number.

parameters.name: domain
parameters.description: List of candidate configurations, a region, or a sampler function.

tools.notes: Introduced in 11.0. For cheap smooth objectives NMinimize/FindMinimum are far faster.

tools.name: NBodySimulation
tools.description: Simulates the motion of a system of particles under a pairwise potential ("InverseSquare" gravity, "Coulomb", "Harmonic", "LennardJones", or a custom potential) from initial positions, velocities and masses, returning an NBodySimulationData object with trajectories that can be plotted, animated or exported. A convenient wrapper over NDSolve for celestial mechanics and molecular-dynamics style demos.
tools.usage:
NBodySimulation["InverseSquare", {<|"Mass" -> m1, "Position" -> p1, "Velocity" -> v1|>, ...}, tmax]
NBodySimulation[{"Custom", potential}, particles, tmax]
data[All, "Position", t]

parameters.name: particles
parameters.description: List of associations with Mass, Position, Velocity (and Charge).

tools.example:
sim = NBodySimulation["InverseSquare", {<|"Mass" -> 1, "Position" -> {0, 0}, "Velocity" -> {0, 0}|>, <|"Mass" -> 0.001, "Position" -> {1, 0}, "Velocity" -> {0, 1}|>}, 20];
ParametricPlot[Evaluate[sim[All, "Position", t]], {t, 0, 20}]

tools.name: Compiled
tools.description: Option of NDSolve, NIntegrate, FindRoot, FindMinimum, Plot and others controlling whether the function being evaluated is compiled to machine code (True/False/Automatic). Set Compiled -> False when the function uses arbitrary precision, symbolic branches or external calls that cannot compile, to avoid CompiledFunction::cfsa warnings and silent fallbacks.
tools.usage:
NIntegrate[f[x], {x, 0, 1}, Compiled -> False]
NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, 1}, Compiled -> True]
tools.example: NIntegrate[BesselJ[0, x] Exp[-x], {x, 0, Infinity}, WorkingPrecision -> 30, Compiled -> False]

tools.name: NormFunction
tools.description: Option of NDSolve (and FindFit, FindMinimum residual methods) giving the norm used to estimate errors and control step size (default an infinity-type norm scaled per component). Change it, e.g. to a scaled 2-norm, when components differ wildly in magnitude; "ScaleFactors"/ error scaling can also be tuned through the norm.
tools.usage:
NDSolve[eqs, y, {t, 0, T}, NormFunction -> (Norm[#, 2] &)]
NDSolve[eqs, y, range, NormFunction -> (Max[Abs[#/scale]] &)]

tools.name: InitialSeeding
tools.description: NDSolve option (12.x) supplying an initial guess for boundary-value problems solved by shooting/collocation ("Shooting", "Chasing" methods); together with Method -> {"Shooting", "StartingInitialConditions" -> ...} it controls BVP solving, where NDSolve otherwise picks a default that may miss the desired solution branch.
tools.usage:
NDSolve[{eqs, y[a] == ya, y[b] == yb}, y, {x, a, b}, InitialSeeding -> {y[a] == guess}]
NDSolve[bvp, y, {x, a, b}, Method -> {"Shooting", "StartingInitialConditions" -> {y[a] == ya, y'[a] == s0}}]
tools.example: NDSolve[{y''[x] + Exp[y[x]] == 0, y[0] == 0, y[1] == 0}, y, {x, 0, 1}, Method -> {"Shooting", "StartingInitialConditions" -> {y[0] == 0, y'[0] == 5}}] (* upper branch of Bratu problem *)

tools.name: MaxIterations
tools.description: Option bounding the number of iterations in FindRoot, FindMinimum, FindFit, NMinimize, FixedPoint, NestWhile, Nearest-style iterative solvers and NetTrain; when hit, a ::cvmit or ::maxit message is issued and the current (possibly unconverged) result returned. Raise it for slowly converging problems, or lower it to bound run time in parameter sweeps.
tools.usage:
FindRoot[eq, {x, x0}, MaxIterations -> 500]
NMinimize[f, vars, MaxIterations -> 1000]
FixedPoint[f, x0, 100] (* positional limit *)
tools.example: FindMinimum[Total[(model[a, b] - data)^2], {{a, 1}, {b, 1}}, MaxIterations -> 1000, Method -> "LevenbergMarquardt"]
